sections.title: Sex and Power in the Middle East: Unveiling Women's Lives
sections.description: How did Middle Eastern women and men really live? What impact did tradition have on practices of veiling, seclusion, and politics? How did attitudes toward intimacy and sexuality change over time? This course strives to answer these questions by offering a comparative perspective on people's lives in the modern Middle East (Southwest Asia) and North Africa. We begin in the 19th century and move quickly to the twentieth century when social policies and politics shaped gender relations. We will consider the birth and popularity of fashion industries, beauty contests, journalism, the visual arts, television, and challenges to norms of sexuality. Part of the class will also engage with traditionalist rejection of such new social and cultural trends. From Iran to Algeria, women and men grappled with culture wars that centered on gender, sexuality, and power. To make the learning process interactive, we will watch video clips, documentaries, and interviews as we delve into this ongoing tug-of-war.

sections.title: Sovereignty and Sexuality: Gender and Power in Society
sections.description: Women in Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) – then as now – lived far less glamorous lives than what some writers, visitors, and “Orientalists” imagined. To understand their actual experiences, this course will grapple with this regional history through global networks and processes. We will consider positionality and identity, including race, ethnicity, and economic status. This was an era in which Western women traveled more frequently to parts of SWANA. We will gauge women’s attitudes (both indigenous and non-indigenous) toward veiling, politics, and secular change while avoiding generalizations. To what extent did family dynamics and sexuality inform social interactions? This course considers such questions by offering a comparative perspective on women’s lives, primarily through memoirs, travelogues, photography, other first-hand accounts, and secondary sources. It combines historical accounts with select fictional works to study women’s social and cultural milieux under colonialism, the evolution of women’s roles in politics and society as the global map changed, and how local communities tied themselves to global solidarity networks. By crossing national boundaries, this course highlights the rich diversity of women's experiences. We will examine the importance or imposition of motherhood; LGBTQ experiences and forms of activism; and women’s roles in revolutionary upheavals.
